q: how to unclog a toilet
how to fix a clogged toilet
toilet won't drain
how to unclog a toilet without a plunger
a: The plunger first: use a flange (toilet) plunger — the kind with the rubber flap — not a flat sink plunger. Position it in the bowl over the drain, and push slowly at first to expel air, then pump firmly 10-15 times; the seal is what makes it work. If that fails: (1) Hot water + dish soap — pour a cup of dish soap and a pot of hot (not boiling) water into the bowl, wait 10-15 minutes, then flush; the soap lubricates and the heat softens the clog. (2) The bucket method — if the bowl is full and rising, bail water out first (you want to avoid an overflow), then apply the plunger. (3) A closet auger (toilet snake) — feed the cable into the trap and crank; this clears what plungers can't (the classic culprit: too much toilet paper, or a flushed object). Never use chemical drain cleaners in a toilet — they don't work on the trap, can damage the wax ring and porcelain, and create hazardous fumes when mixed. If it's still clogged after the auger, or the toilet overflows/leaks at the base, the issue may be the wax ring or a main-line blockage — call a plumber; a main-line clog is no longer a DIY toilet job. The prevention: 'flushable' wipes are not actually flushable — they're the #1 modern cause of clogs, along with paper towels and excessive toilet paper.

q: how to fix a squeaky door
how to stop a door from squeaking
squeaky hinge fix
how to lubricate door hinges
a: The fix is lubricating the hinges — the squeak is metal-on-metal friction where the hinge pin rides. The best option: a spray lubricant with a straw attachment (WD-40 works in a pinch but evaporates — a silicone or white-lithium grease lasts far longer). Open the door, spray into the top of each hinge where the pin meets the barrel, then work the door back and forth 5-10 times to work the lubricant in; wipe off any drips. The classic alternative when you have no lubricant: a pencil — rub the pencil lead (graphite) on the hinge pin or drop pencil shavings into the hinge top; graphite is a dry lubricant and works surprisingly well. If it still squeaks: the hinge pin may be worn — remove the pin (tap it out with a screwdriver and hammer from the bottom), wipe it clean, and apply lithium grease, or replace the pin with a slightly larger one. Another cause: a hinge that's loose or misaligned — tighten the hinge screws (a stripped screw hole can be fixed with a wooden toothpick/matches and glue in the hole, or a slightly longer screw), and if the door is rubbing on the frame, adjust the hinge. One more subtle cause: the door is dragging on the floor or frame — then it's not the hinge but the door edge, which needs planing. The 2-minute version: spray, swing, done — most squeaks are solved that simply.

q: how to patch a hole in the wall
how to fix a hole in drywall
how to repair a small hole in the wall
how to fix a nail hole
a: The method depends on hole size: (1) Small holes (nail/screw): fill with spackle — a dab with a putty knife, let it dry (15-30 min for lightweight spackle), sand smooth with fine sandpaper, and touch up with paint. (2) Medium holes (up to ~15 cm / 6 in): use a patch — cut a piece of drywall mesh patch or fiberglass tape slightly larger than the hole, stick it over the hole, apply joint compound over it with a putty knife (thin coats, 2-3, letting each dry), sand, and paint. (3) Large holes (doorknob-sized and bigger): cut the hole into a clean rectangle, screw a piece of wood or drywall backer behind it, cut a drywall patch to fit, screw it to the backer, then tape the seams and compound as above — or use a 'California patch' (a drywall piece with paper overhang, glued over the hole with compound). The universal steps: prep (remove loose drywall, clean dust), fill (in thin layers — a big glob shrinks and cracks), dry, sand (smooth, feathering the edges), prime if you used joint compound on bare paper, and paint. The two beginner mistakes: applying compound too thick (cracks on drying) and skipping the primer (the patch shows through as a dull spot even after painting). For textured walls, matching the texture is the final step — a spray texture can or a sponge dab works for orange-peel.

q: how to hang shelves on drywall
how to mount shelves on drywall
how to hang a shelf without studs
how to anchor a shelf to drywall
a: The load decides the method: (1) Light shelves (decor, small books) — drywall anchors: for 10-25 kg, plastic expansion anchors (just drill a pilot hole, tap in, screw); for 25-45 kg, hollow-wall anchors like 'toggle bolts' (drill a hole, insert the folded toggle, tighten) or self-drilling 'snap toggles' — the toggle spreads a wide flange behind the drywall, which is what carries the weight. (2) Heavy shelves (large books, TVs, anything valuable) — find the studs and screw into them: a stud finder (or the trick: knock for solid spots, or look for outlet boxes — studs are typically 40 cm / 16 in apart from them); screw the bracket into the stud with wood screws — two studs is much stronger than one. A shelf bracket needs at least two anchors/brackets, spread apart, not clustered in the middle. The critical rule: drywall alone (just the paper and gypsum, no anchor) holds almost nothing — a screw in bare drywall pulls out under a few kilos. Toggle anchors are rated by weight: read the package and pick anchors rated above your actual load (a safety margin of 2x is wise). The sign you got it wrong: the anchor spins when you tighten the screw — it's stripped and won't hold; move to a larger anchor or find a stud. For anything fragile or expensive (TVs, kids' furniture), the rule is simple: studs or a proper wall, never anchors alone — anchors fail catastrophically, not gradually.

q: how to fix a stuck window
how to fix a window that won't open
window stuck closed how to open
how to free a stuck window
a: First, diagnose why it's stuck: (1) Painted shut — the most common: run a utility knife along the seam between the window and the frame on all sides to cut the paint seal (you may also need to tap the frame with a hammer and a block of wood). (2) Swollen sash — wood windows swell in humid weather: try opening from the top, run a knife around the edges, and sand the high spots where the sash rubs. (3) Warped or misaligned — check the tracks: if the sash is crooked, it jams; loosen the sash, realign it, and retighten. (4) Debris in the track — vacuum or clean the channels (dirt and paint chips jam sliders). (5) A broken balance (double-hung windows) — if the window moves but won't stay or is hard to move, the spring balance or cord is broken; this is a replaceable part (windows have accessible balances in most modern units). Technique for stuck double-hungs: lift from the center bottom (pulling one corner makes it cock and jam harder), and use a small pry bar or putty knife to break the seal around the edges — never force it with a big screwdriver against the glass. After freeing it, lubricate the tracks with silicone spray (not oil — it attracts dirt). If a window is painted shut AND sealed tight, cutting the paint with a knife before prying prevents cracked glass and frame damage. If it's a newer vinyl window that won't slide, check the locking mechanism isn't engaged and the sash isn't dropped off its track.

q: how to caulk a bathtub
how to re caulk a bathtub
how to seal a bathtub
how to fix moldy caulk in the shower
a: Re-caulking a tub properly: (1) Remove the old caulk completely — the #1 mistake is caulking over old caulk. Cut it out with a utility knife or a caulk remover tool, pull it up, and clean any remaining residue with rubbing alcohol or a caulk remover; the surface must be dry and clean (let it dry 24h if the tub was wet). (2) Choose the right caulk: use 100% silicone (or a labeled tub-and-tile silicone) — NOT acrylic/water-based 'kitchen and bath' caulk, which is what molds and peels in showers; silicone is waterproof, flexible, and mold-resistant. (3) Apply: cut the tube tip at a 45° angle, slightly smaller than the gap, and run a steady bead along the joint where tub meets tile, holding the gun at 45°. (4) Smooth it: the classic method — dip your finger (or a caulk-smoothing tool) in soapy water and run it along the bead to press it into the joint and make a clean concave line; wipe excess on a rag. (5) Let it cure: silicone takes 24 hours to fully cure — no showers in the meantime (check the label). (6) Mold prevention: ventilate after showers (fan or window) and wipe down the caulk lines; when mold does appear, clean with a bleach-free mold cleaner — and when it keeps coming back, the caulk has lost its seal and it's time to re-do it. The tell that the seal is gone: water gets behind the caulk (the tile darkens or the wall behind gets wet) — that's when re-caulking is urgent, because the damage behind the tile is worse than the cosmetic mold.

q: how to fix a garbage disposal
garbage disposal not working
how to reset a garbage disposal
garbage disposal humming but not spinning
a: The most common failure — humming but not spinning — is almost always a jam, and there's a built-in fix: (1) Turn off the power at the breaker or unplug it (safety first — never put your hand in a disposal). (2) Reset the overload button: look under the unit for a small red button and press it — the disposal's thermal overload trips when it's overheated; if it was humming, it probably tripped. (3) Free the jam: with the power OFF, insert a hex wrench (Allen key) into the hex hole on the underside of the disposal and turn it back and forth to manually rotate the blades and free whatever's stuck; many disposals come with the wrench clipped to the side. (4) Once it turns freely, press reset, restore power, and run cold water while it spins. If it doesn't hum at all: check the wall switch, the breaker, and the reset button; if there's a plug under the sink, check it. If it leaks instead of jamming: tighten the connections (the sink flange, the dishwasher hose connection — check the rubber gaskets). Prevention: run cold water while grinding (hot water melts fat, which congeals and clogs), never put fibrous material (celery, onion skins, potato peels), grease, or large bones down, and grind citrus peels occasionally to clean. When the jam won't clear, or the motor runs but the blades won't turn even after the wrench — the motor may be burnt out, and a replacement (an easy swap for a DIYer, ~1 hour) is usually cheaper than a repair call.
